questions.question: A student stirs a spoonful of grey iron filings into a dish of pale sand until the two are mixed all through. Then she sweeps a strong magnet slowly over the dish. What happens?
questions.answer: The iron clings to it, and the sand stays
choices: The iron clings to it, and the sand stays
The iron and the sand both cling to it
Nothing clings, for mixing changed the iron
Nothing clings, for the sand blocks the pull
questions.context: In a mixture each substance keeps its own properties, so the iron is still magnetic, and the magnet pulls the filings out of the sand. Pale sand is mostly quartz, which a magnet does not pull, and it does not stop the magnet reaching the iron.
questions.grade_note: TEKS 5.6B asks 5th graders to show that some mixtures keep the properties of their parts, and iron filings and sand is the standard's own example.

questions.question: A geologist pours a scoop of dry sand and gravel from a riverbank into a stack of sieves and shakes it hard. Each sieve ends up holding a different part of the scoop. What does the stack sort the grains by?
choices: Their size
Their weight
Their hardness
Their kind of rock
questions.context: A sieve sorts by size: grains smaller than its holes fall through, and bigger ones stay behind. The top sieve has the biggest holes, so pebbles stay there while finer and finer sand drops to the sieves below. A grain small enough for the holes drops through, heavy or light, whatever rock it is made of; weighing what each sieve holds comes afterwards.
questions.grade_note: Separating mixtures with screens and sieves opens FOSS's grade-5 Mixtures and Solutions module, and England's Year 5 (ages 9-10) names sieving among the ways to separate a mixture.

questions.question: A student stirs a mixture of sand and salt into a beaker of water. Then she pours it all through a funnel lined with filter paper. What is left behind on the filter paper?
choices: Only the sand
Only the salt
Both the sand and the salt
Nothing at all
questions.context: The salt dissolves into bits far too small to see, and they slip through the paper's tiny holes along with the water. The sand grains are too big, so they stay on the paper. A filter cannot take salt out of salt water; to get the salt back, the water that drips through must be dried away.
questions.grade_note: FOSS's grade-5 module has students find that a filter catches undissolved solids but cannot separate salt from water, and the RSC runs the same sand-and-salt practical for ages 9-11.

questions.question: A chemist stirs bright blue crystals of copper sulfate into a flask of clear water until the crystals are gone and all the water has turned pale blue. She seals the flask and leaves it on a shelf for a month. Where is the blue colour then?
questions.answer: Spread evenly all through the water
choices: Spread evenly all through the water
Settled in a dark layer at the bottom
Risen in a dark layer at the top
Gone, leaving the water clear again
questions.context: The copper sulfate has made a solution: its bits are spread evenly through the water and are far too small to settle, however long the flask stands. Sand or mud stirred into water is different, because its grains are big enough to sink to the bottom.
questions.grade_note: 5th graders learn that a solution is mixed evenly all through (TEKS 5.6C compares substances before and after they form a solution), unlike sand in water, which settles.

questions.question: A student stirs salt into a jar of water a spoonful at a time, and each spoonful disappears. At last one spoonful stays on the bottom, however long she stirs. Why does this last spoonful not dissolve?
questions.answer: The water holds all the salt it can
choices: The water holds all the salt it can
The last spoonful is heavier than the rest
The salt sank too fast to be dissolved
The salt has lost its power to dissolve
questions.context: Water can dissolve only so much salt, about 36 grams in every 100 grams of water at room temperature. A solution that holds all it can is called saturated, and any more salt added just sits on the bottom.
questions.grade_note: FOSS's grade-5 Mixtures and Solutions module has students add salt to water until no more will dissolve, making a saturated solution.

questions.question: A road crew spreads salt over an icy road on a winter morning, when the air is at -5 degrees Celsius. Within an hour the ice has turned to wet slush. Why does the ice melt?
questions.answer: Salt water stays liquid at that temperature
choices: Salt water stays liquid at that temperature
Salt gives off heat as it dissolves
Salt soaks the cold out of the ice
Salt reacts with ice to make a new substance
questions.context: Pure water freezes at 0 degrees Celsius, but salt water must be colder still before it freezes; seawater freezes only at about -1.8 degrees. Salt dissolves into water on the ice, and the salt water stays liquid at -5 degrees, so the ice it touches melts into slush. Dissolving salt gives off no heat, and the slush is only ice and salt water, with nothing new made.
questions.grade_note: The grade-5 line asks that a dissolved solid makes a solution with properties unlike its parts (TEKS 5.6C), and salt water's lower freezing point is the everyday case behind road salt.

questions.question: A student weighs a beaker of water and a dish of salt together on a balance. She tips the salt into the water and stirs until no salt can be seen, then sets the empty dish back beside the beaker. What does the balance show now?
choices: The same mass as before
A little less mass than before
A little more mass than before
Only the mass of the water and dish
questions.context: The dissolved salt is still in the water, in bits too small to see, so it still has mass: 150 grams of water and 10 grams of salt make 160 grams of salt water. No mass is lost when one substance dissolves in another.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-PS1-2 asks 5th graders to show that the total weight of matter is conserved when substances dissolve, even when one seems to vanish.

questions.question: A student pours water into a plastic bottle, screws the cap on tight, marks the water level and weighs the bottle. She leaves it in a freezer overnight, and by morning the water is solid ice. What has changed about the water?
questions.answer: Its volume, but not its mass
choices: Its volume, but not its mass
Its mass, but not its volume
Both its mass and its volume
Neither its mass nor its volume
questions.context: Freezing adds no water and takes none away, so the bottle weighs exactly what it did. But water swells by about 9 percent as it freezes, so the ice stands above the mark. Ice floats because it takes up more room for its mass, not because it weighs less than the water it came from.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-PS1-2 names changes of state among the changes that conserve weight, and the grade-5 Inquiry Project teaches that frozen water weighs the same though its volume grows.

questions.question: An iron nail lies out in the rain for weeks and grows a flaky, reddish-brown coat of rust. When the nail is scraped, the rust crumbles away like dry dust. What is the rust?
questions.answer: A new substance made from the iron
choices: A new substance made from the iron
The same iron with a new colour
Dried mud stuck onto the iron
Iron and rainwater mixed together
questions.context: Iron joins with oxygen from the air, helped by water, to make rust, a new substance with new properties: reddish-brown, crumbly and far weaker than iron. Unlike a mixture, rust cannot be turned back into iron by drying it or picking it apart.
questions.grade_note: NGSS 5-PS1-4 asks 5th graders whether a change makes a new substance, and rusting is the standard first example (England's Year 5 guidance names it too).
